title: Quebec rallies behind Montreal’s bid for global defence bank headquarters | CBC News
html:
Montreal

Quebec rallies behind Montreal’s bid for global defence bank headquarters

Cities have until Dec. 3 to submit their applications to host proposed NATO institution

Montreal is competing to host the headquarters of the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB), and Quebec's sovereignist government has thrown its full support behind the bid.

At city hall on Monday, Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon joined Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada to formally back the metropolis's candidacy and highlight its qualifications for the multilateral institution.

The DSRB is designed to finance defence, security, and resilience projects for NATO members and allied nations. Canada has committed to NATO's defence spending target of five per cent of GDP by 2035.

Ottawa, Toronto, and Vancouver are also competing to host the bank. Interested cities have until Dec. 3 to submit their applications, and the federal government will make the final decision on the headquarters' location.

Describing Montreal as a "globetrotting city," St-Pierre Plamondon touted its multilingual talent pool, noting that "28 per cent of the [city's] population masters three languages."

"When you look at the criteria applicable to that project, we have all the arguments to win this, and we are all together — Quebec as a whole," St-Pierre Plamondon said.

Martinez Ferrada said securing backing from the provincial government was a critical step.

"It was the last piece for putting forward our candidacy that I know we can win," she said.

Meanwhile, in Ottawa, Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet brushed off the suggestion that Quebec's sovereignist government would hinder Montreal's chances of landing the project.

"As long as Quebecers pay their share of taxes, they are entitled to the same consideration as anyone else," Blanchet said. "And if Montreal is so well positioned, it is because Montreal is in an enviable international position, namely as a privileged bridge to Europe. No change in status will change that."

The federal government wants to reduce its reliance on U.S. military equipment and increase the share of its Canadian equipment acquisitions to 70 per cent within 10 years . (Antoine Allain/Radio-Canada)

In April, Canada was selected to host the DSRB headquarters following negotiations with European partners.

Of the nine countries participating in the project so far, Canada is the only G7 member, according to the federal Finance Ministry.

Canada tried in vain for months to persuade the U.K. to join, though the latter opted to put in place its own defence-financing initiative.

Representatives of the founding countries are scheduled to meet on Nov. 30 in Luxembourg to sign the bank's articles of agreement.

Martinez Ferrada set her sights on bringing the bank to Montreal shortly after taking office in November 2025.

She and former Quebec premier François Legault placed the bid at the top of the agenda during their first official meeting, arguing that Montreal — which already hosts 68 international organizations, including six United Nations offices — would be a natural fit for the DSRB.

Legault previously estimated that the new bank would create 3,500 jobs.

With files from Radio-Canada
summary: Montreal is competing to host the headquarters of the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB), and Quebec's sovereignist government has thrown its full support behind the bid.
